title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
summary: Carbonyl compounds contain the >C=O group (sp² carbon, polar, planar). Aldehydes (R–CHO) and ketones (R–CO–R'). Preparation of aldehydes: oxidation of primary alcohols (PCC), dehydrogenation, Rosenmund reduction of acid chlorides (H2/Pd–BaSO4), Stephen reaction (RCN + SnCl2/HCl then H2O) and ozonolysis of alkenes; ketones: oxidation of secondary alcohols, hydration of alkynes, Friedel–Crafts acylation, and Grignard reagent with nitriles. Reactions: nucleophilic addition (HCN gives cyanohydrin, NaHSO3 gives bisulphite compound, alcohols give hemiacetal/acetal; aldehydes are more reactive than ketones due to less steric hindrance and greater positive charge on carbon), addition–elimination with ammonia derivatives (NH2OH gives oxime, NH2NH2 hydrazone, 2,4-DNP gives red-orange precipitate, semicarbazide gives semicarbazone), reduction to alcohols (NaBH4, LiAlH4), Clemmensen reduction (Zn–Hg/conc. HCl) and Wolff–Kishner reduction (NH2NH2/KOH, ethylene glycol) to alkanes: C=O → CH2. Aldehydes with α-hydrogen undergo aldol condensation in dilute alkali (2CH3CHO → CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO, 3-hydroxybutanal, which on heating gives but-2-enal); aldehydes without α-hydrogen (HCHO, benzaldehyde) undergo Cannizzaro reaction in conc. alkali (2HCHO + NaOH → CH3OH + HCOONa). Tests: aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent (silver mirror) and Fehling's solution (red Cu2O) and give a pink colour with Schiff's reagent, whereas ketones do not; methyl ketones and ethanal give the iodoform test (yellow CHI3).

Carboxylic acids (R–COOH) have the carboxyl group; they form hydrogen-bonded dimers and have high boiling points; the solubility of lower acids in water decreases with chain length (HCOOH > CH3COOH > ... ; aromatic acids are poorly soluble). Preparation: oxidation of primary alcohols and aldehydes, hydrolysis of nitriles and amides, carboxylation of Grignard reagents, and oxidation of alkylbenzenes by alkaline KMnO4 (toluene → benzoic acid). Acidity: the carboxylate ion is stabilised by resonance, so pKa is about 4–5; electron-withdrawing groups (–Cl, –NO2) increase acidity (ClCH2COOH > CH3COOH; HCOOH > CH3COOH). Reactions: salt formation (with NaHCO3 gives CO2 effervescence – test for acids), esterification (RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H2O, conc. H2SO4), acid chlorides (with SOCl2, PCl5), acid anhydrides (heating two molecules with P2O5, or acid chloride + sodium carboxylate: 2CH3COOH + P2O5 → (CH3CO)2O), amides (with NH3 then heat), reduction with LiAlH4 to primary alcohols, decarboxylation (soda lime gives alkane), and the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction – α-halogenation using Cl2 or Br2/red P: CH3COOH → ClCH2COOH.

Methanal (formalin, 37–40% aqueous) preserves biological specimens and makes bakelite; ethanal is used for acetic acid and drugs; acetone is a solvent; benzaldehyde is used in perfumes; formic acid in leather and rubber industry; acetic acid (vinegar, 5–8%) in food and as a solvent; benzoic acid as a food preservative; long-chain acids as soaps.

April 2025
Why is carboxylic acid more acidic than phenol?

The carboxylate ion is stabilised by resonance with the negative charge shared equally between two electronegative oxygens, whereas in the phenoxide ion the charge is spread onto less electronegative carbons.
Why do carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than alcohols of similar mass?
They form stable hydrogen-bonded dimers (two H-bonds between two molecules) in addition to higher polarity.
sa: Arrange the acids CH3COOH, HCOOH, p-ClC6H4COOH and CH3(CH2)3COOH in the increasing order of their solubility in water.

p-ClC6H4COOH < CH3(CH2)3COOH < CH3COOH < HCOOH. Solubility falls as the hydrocarbon part (and the aromatic ring) becomes larger because hydrogen bonding with water is outweighed by the hydrophobic part.
Describe a chemical test to distinguish aldehydes from ketones with equations.
Tollens' test: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3OH− → RCOO− + 2Ag↓ + 4NH3 + 2H2O (silver mirror); ketones do not react. Fehling's test: aldehyde gives red-brown Cu2O; ketones do not.
Explain the nucleophilic addition of HCN to a carbonyl compound with the mechanism.

CN− attacks the electron-deficient carbonyl carbon to give an alkoxide, which takes H+ to give a cyanohydrin: CH3CHO + HCN → CH3CH(OH)CN. Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones because of less steric hindrance and a more positive carbon.
Write the reaction of acetic acid with (a) PCl5 (b) NH3 and heat (c) LiAlH4.
(a) CH3COOH + PCl5 → CH3COCl + POCl3 + HCl. (b) CH3COOH + NH3 → CH3COONH4 → (heat) CH3CONH2 + H2O. (c) CH3COOH → (LiAlH4) CH3CH2OH.
Explain the Wolff–Kishner reduction and compare it with the Clemmensen reduction.

Wolff–Kishner: the carbonyl compound forms a hydrazone with NH2NH2 which is heated with KOH in ethylene glycol to give the alkane (C=O → CH2). Clemmensen uses Zn–Hg/conc. HCl (acidic medium) and is unsuitable for acid-sensitive compounds, while Wolff–Kishner is in basic medium.
Explain the acidic strength of carboxylic acids with the effect of substituents.

The carboxylate is resonance stabilised, so acids are stronger than alcohols; electron-withdrawing groups (–Cl, –NO2) stabilise the anion and increase acidity (ClCH2COOH > CH3COOH), electron-donating alkyl groups decrease it (HCOOH > CH3COOH).
la: (a) Give the chemical equations for (i) Clemmensen reduction (ii) Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction (iii) aldol condensation. (b) (i) Which reagents are used to prepare acid anhydrides from carboxylic acids? (ii) Write the equation for the formation of a symmetrical acid anhydride.

(a) (i) CH3COCH3 → (Zn–Hg, HCl) CH3CH2CH3. (ii) CH3COOH + Cl2 (red P) → ClCH2COOH + HCl. (iii) 2CH3CHO → (dil. NaOH) CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO.
(b) (i) Dehydrating agents: P2O5 (or acid chloride with sodium carboxylate). (ii) 2CH3COOH → (CH3CO)2O + H2O with P2O5.

(a) Distinguish between aldehydes and ketones by a chemical test and give equations. (b) Give the equations for (i) the formation of an oxime of an aldehyde (ii) the Cannizzaro reaction. (c) Arrange HCOOH, CH3COOH, CH3(CH2)3COOH in increasing order of water solubility.

(a) Tollens' reagent: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3OH− → RCOO− + 2Ag + 4NH3 + 2H2O (ketones do not respond).
(b) (i) CH3CHO + NH2OH → CH3CH=NOH + H2O. (ii) 2HCHO + NaOH → CH3OH + HCOONa.
(c) CH3(CH2)3COOH < CH3COOH < HCOOH.
(a) What is aldol condensation? Write the mechanism for ethanal. (b) State the conditions for the Cannizzaro reaction and compare it with aldol condensation.

(a) Aldehydes or ketones having α-hydrogen condense in dilute base to give β-hydroxy carbonyl compounds. Mechanism: OH− removes an α-H from CH3CHO to give the enolate −CH2CHO, which attacks the carbonyl carbon of another CH3CHO, forming CH3CH(O−)CH2CHO; protonation gives 3-hydroxybutanal, which dehydrates on heating to but-2-enal.
(b) Cannizzaro: aldehydes without α-hydrogen (HCHO, C6H5CHO) with conc. NaOH – one molecule is oxidised to carboxylate and the other reduced to alcohol. Aldol needs α-hydrogen and dilute alkali.

(a) How is acetic anhydride prepared? (b) Describe the reactions of carboxylic acids: esterification, with NaHCO3, with PCl5 and decarboxylation. (c) Write one use each of formic acid and acetic acid.

(a) By heating acetic acid with P2O5 or from acetyl chloride and sodium acetate.
(b) RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H2O (H2SO4); RCOOH + NaHCO3 → RCOONa + CO2 + H2O; RCOOH + PCl5 → RCOCl + POCl3 + HCl; RCOONa + NaOH (soda lime) → R–H + Na2CO3.
(c) Formic acid in leather tanning and rubber coagulation; acetic acid as vinegar for food.
